parsed_answer.content: In Java Persistence Architecture (JPA) and Hibernate, managing bidirectional relationships requires determining which entity holds the database foreign key constraint. This is known as the owning side of a relationship, while the opposite side is designated as the inverse or non-owning side using the mappedBy attribute. The owning side is strictly responsible for synchronizing state changes to the database during flush time; updates made exclusively on the mappedBy side are ignored by the persistence context. When a many-to-many relationship—or a complex unidirectional/bidirectional one-to-many or many-to-one mapping—cannot cleanly store a foreign key on either of the participating entity tables without violating normalization, JPA introduces a join table. A join table is a dedicated associative database table containing foreign keys pointing to the primary keys of both participating entities, effectively bridging the multi-valued association without altering the primary entity schemas.

items: The mappedBy attribute signals to the Hibernate metadata parser that the field is mapped by the referenced property in the target entity, meaning no redundant foreign key column is generated in the table of the inverse class.
When dealing with a join table in a Many-to-Many association, the owning side dictates which entity controls the insertion and deletion of rows inside the intermediate cross-reference table.

Failing to update both sides of a bidirectional in-memory object graph before committing a transaction leads to first-level cache discrepancies, where the entity manager returns stale collections despite successful database flushes.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production bug occurs when developers populate only the inverse side of a bidirectional relationship (e.g., calling author.getBooks().add(book)) without setting book.setAuthor(author). Because Hibernate only inspects the owning side (Book.author) during flush time, the foreign key column remains null in the database, resulting in a constraint violation or silently dropped relationship depending on nullability rules.
